title: Breaking Up with Google Play: Why Conversations Is Now Free
why: A solo developer who sustained himself on Play Store sales for over a decade walked away entirely, showing how EU research grants (NLnet, European Commission, funded through 2029) can replace app-store revenue for a federated messaging client.
notes: Conversations, a federated (XMPP) Android messaging client, launched March 24, 2014 on a paid-binary/open-source model that was the developer's primary income for over ten years.
Google's 15% cut ran the author over 1000 Euro/year, which he notes is about 1.5x his internet bill, with no way to reach a human for support.
The app was removed from the Play Store twice, once on what he says was a false accusation of uploading users' contacts, not tied to any specific update.

Current update review wait is 14 days and worsening; he blames an avalanche of AI-generated slop apps, and warns Google makes no distinction between feature and security updates, so security fixes get delayed too.
Funding is now secured via NLnet and European Commission grants through end of 2029, removing his economic dependency on Play Store revenue.
F-Droid is now the primary distribution channel; the APK is built reproducibly and signed with his personal key. All figures and claims are the author's own, self-reported.
summary: The developer of Conversations, a federated XMPP messaging client for Android launched in March 2014, explains why he is making the app free and abandoning Google Play. For over a decade the paid-binary open-source model was his main income, with steady Play Store revenue supplementing paid development, consulting, and later grants. He details grievances: a 15% Google cut costing him over 1000 Euro/year, no human support, two removals from the store (one on a false contact-upload accusation), and a current 14-day review wait he attributes partly to AI-generated app slop clogging the queue, which also delays security updates. Having secured grant funding via NLnet and the European Commission through the end of 2029, he says he is no longer economically dependent on Google and is moving distribution to F-Droid, where the APK is built reproducibly and signed with his personal key. All claims and figures are self-reported.
novelty: dev ditches Play Store entirely after 12 years, goes grant-funded
audience: indie/open-source developers weighing app store economics and distribution

title: Benchmarking Wild vs Mold
why: Mold's published numbers put Wild up to ~1.3x slower, but the gap is mostly benchmark config (output-file deletion, --no-fork, filesystem) plus Mold's own 2.42.x speedups, not a raw regression in Wild.
notes: On clang-release, config alone swings Wild's time: ext4+delete+no-fork gives 1.0x vs Mold (0.21s), while Wild's historical tmpfs+no-delete+fork gives 0.6x (0.11s vs Mold's 0.19s). Mold's number barely moves across configs.

Wild's past benchmarks reused an existing output file on tmpfs with forking enabled; Mold deletes the output between runs, passes --no-fork, and uses ext4. The author concedes tmpfs was probably a mistake and will test both going forward.

Wild lacks Mold's OS-specific file-write tweaks (fallocate to pre-allocate, hugepages to map the output), described in the 'mold: A Massively Parallel Linker' paper; both are already added to Wild and ship next release.
Mold's 2.42.0/2.42.1 releases, which landed after Wild's August 4 benchmarks, brought the main Mold speedups, accounting for much of the apparent Wild regression.

On a 16-core Ryzen 9955HX (92GiB RAM) the author reproduced Mold's M1 Ultra ratios (1.2x blender-debug, 1.2x godot-debug, 0.9x blender-release, 1.0x clang-release) but could not reproduce the larger Threadripper gap; he speculates Wild's 128 threads vs Mold's 32 on that 64-core/384GiB box, calling it guesswork and inviting Threadripper testers.
summary: David Lattimore, author of the Wild linker, investigates why Mold's updated benchmarks show Wild substantially slower than Wild's own August 4 numbers. He identifies three causes: methodology differences (Mold deletes the output file, passes --no-fork, and runs on ext4, while Wild historically reused an existing output on tmpfs with forking), Wild's lack of Mold's OS-specific file-creation optimizations (fallocate pre-allocation and hugepage mapping, both now added and shipping next release), and Mold's own speedups in 2.42.0/2.42.1 that postdated Wild's benchmarks. On clang-release, config changes move Wild's measured time from 0.21s (Mold-style, 1.0x) to 0.11s (Wild-style, 0.6x) while Mold stays near 0.19-0.20s. Running Mold's config on a 16-core Ryzen, he reproduces the M1 Ultra ratios (roughly 0.9x-1.2x) but cannot reproduce the larger 64-core Threadripper gap, speculating it stems from Wild using 128 threads vs Mold's 32. He presents the thread-count theory as unverified guesswork and asks Threadripper owners to test.
novelty: benchmark methodology diffs explain Wild/Mold speed gap, not raw perf
audience: systems engineers and linker/toolchain developers

title: Anthropic’s proposed AI safety bill only kicks in if 50 deaths or $1 billion in damages are on the line
why: If this draft becomes law, Commerce would be the sole agency able to halt a model release, and only after a risk crosses 50 deaths/injuries or $1B in damages, so most model shipping stays untouched by federal pre-release review.
notes: The trigger is narrow: a model release can be blocked only if it risks 50+ deaths or injuries or $1B in damages, scoped to bioweapons, AI-enabled cyberattacks, or a lab losing control of a model or agents.
Enforcement is centralized: per the text, no other U.S. department, agency, or officer could order a lab to stop a release; only the Commerce Department.

Process: an independent evaluator registered with Commerce assesses labs periodically, reports an imminent risk within 72 hours, and Commerce must then present evidence to a federal judge in the D.C. District Court, who decides on halting.
Conflict-of-interest caveat: labs may pay the evaluators, but only if payment does not affect independence; the article gives no mechanism for verifying that.
Anthropic confirms the bill tracks its Advanced AI Framework, pushed to federal and state lawmakers since June; sourcing on the bill text is attributed to Politico.
Competing proposals noted: a congressional effort to mandate kill switches, and Sen. Bernie Sanders proposing a 20-year prison term for building AI superintelligence.
summary: Tom's Hardware, citing Politico, reports Anthropic is lobbying for an AI safety bill that would let the federal government block a model's release only when it risks causing $1 billion in damages or 50+ deaths or injuries, limited to bioweapons, AI-enabled cyberattacks, or loss of control over a model or agents. An independent evaluator registered with the Commerce Department would periodically assess labs and could be paid by the lab provided independence is preserved; on finding imminent risk it would report to Commerce within 72 hours, after which Commerce would bring evidence before a federal judge in the D.C. District Court to decide on halting the release. The draft would make Commerce the only body able to order a lab to stop a release, preempting other agencies. Anthropic says the bill reflects its Advanced AI Framework, advocated to lawmakers since June. The article frames this against competing measures, including a push for mandatory kill switches and Sen. Bernie Sanders' proposed 20-year prison term for developing AI superintelligence. The piece also recounts several dramatic AI-incident claims (an OpenAI model escaping its test environment, a failed kill switch, self-replicating worms) that it presents without independent verification.
novelty: Anthropic's draft bill sets threshold at 50 deaths or $1B damages
audience: AI policy watchers and engineers tracking regulatory frameworks

title: The Decoherence Trap: When AI slop drowns out the signal in an endless sea of noise
why: If your team is shipping AI-generated code into an existing codebase, three cited studies say you are trading a 30% jump in code volume for 49% longer reviews and lasting complexity, not more finished work.
notes: Defines 'decoherence' as the accumulation of locally valid but mutually incompatible or redundant models in a system, where the cost of change comes to be dominated by translating among them and preventing side effects; the author frames it as worse than ordinary tech debt.

Key claim: decoherence grows with the rate of change, not the passage of time, and compounds (each sloppy change makes the next harder), producing runaway exponential growth; a frozen codebase stays exactly as decoherent as you left it.

Cited Harvard study of 718 companies: adopting coding agents raised code written by 30% with no measurable increase in finished work; pull requests took 49% longer to review and nearly twice as many were sent back for changes.

Cited Carnegie Mellon study of open-source projects adopting Cursor: a velocity jump that did not last plus a lasting rise in code complexity, with that complexity itself a major cause of the later slowdown.

Cited analysis of 300,000+ AI-authored commits across 6,000+ repos: about 1 in 11 (up to 1 in 7 depending on the assistant) introduced at least one quality issue, and nearly a quarter of those issues remain in the code.

Argument structure is analogy plus an admittedly arbitrary simulation; the author concedes the model's weights are arbitrary and do not prove how real systems evolve, only that the 'Sweet Spot' curve can emerge from simple local decisions.
summary: This personal-blog essay introduces 'decoherence': the buildup of locally valid but mutually incompatible or redundant models within a system, such that the cost of any change becomes dominated by translating among those models and avoiding side effects. Using an extended analogy of incrementally replacing pipes in a building (and the Ship of Theseus), the author argues that patchwork transitions create a system harder to reason about than either homogeneous system alone, and that this complexity grows with the rate of change rather than over time, compounding under schedule pressure toward a 'Decoherence Collapse.' The author contends this dynamic rules out a runaway recursive self-improvement / intelligence explosion, because decoherence limits how fast AI can improve both in isolation and in the real world, and engages the Software Intelligence Explosion argument of Forethought's Tom Davidson on data bottlenecks and the 'human-quality ceiling.' To argue agents make decoherence worse rather than better, the piece cites a Harvard study of 718 companies (30% more code, no measurable gain in finished work, 49% longer reviews), a Carnegie Mellon study of Cursor-adopting open-source projects (short-lived velocity, lasting added complexity), and an analysis of 300,000+ AI-authored commits (roughly 1 in 11 introducing a quality issue). A browser-based simulation illustrates the 'Sweet Spot' curve, though the author explicitly notes its weights are arbitrary and demonstrate only that the behavior can emerge, not that it must.
novelty: names 'decoherence' as a distinct, worse-than-tech-debt failure mode from AI-accelerated patchwork change
audience: engineers/architects thinking about long-term maintainability of AI-generated code and systems

title: Reverse-engineering the vintage Intel 8087's tangent algorithm: more than CORDIC
why: A transistor-level teardown shows exactly how a 1980 coprocessor hit 64-bit tangent accuracy fast: 16 CORDIC steps for the coarse angle, then a single rational approximation for the tiny remainder, a hybrid worth knowing when you implement transcendentals in constrained hardware.
notes: FPTAN runs in roughly 90 microseconds versus about 13,000 microseconds for the same computation on the bare 8086, per the article.

The algorithm is hybrid: 16 CORDIC iterations give ~2^-16 accuracy, then the leftover angle (around 2^-16) is handled by the Pade approximant 3x/(3-x^2), whose error scales as x^4 and so stays under 2^-64, meeting the chip's 64-bit significand requirement.

FPTAN returns a separate numerator (Y) and denominator (X) rather than the quotient, so the slow division is skipped; CORDIC itself needs only shift, add, subtract, and a precomputed table of angles arctan(2^-n), no multiply or divide.

Three phases: pseudo-division (decide which special angles to subtract, recording 1/0 decision bits in a 16-bit shift register), the rational approximation (its only costly op is a 64-bit square, done via radix-4 Booth multiplication), and pseudo-multiplication (apply rotations smallest-first to cut rounding error).

Findings come from physically decapping an 8087 with a chisel and microscope imaging; the microcode ROM holds 1648 micro-instructions, and FPTAN starts at address #1039. The code uses implicit fixed-point exponents that exist only in the algorithm, not in the chip's registers.

Caveats the author flags: three exponent-based paths (argument returned unchanged if exponent <= -64; CORDIC skipped if <= -17; full CORDIC for -1 to -16), and every nonzero input triggers a 'precision' exception since only tan(0) is computed exactly.
summary: Ken Shirriff reverse-engineers the tangent instruction (FPTAN) of Intel's 1980 8087 floating-point coprocessor by decapping a chip and imaging its die, then reading the microcode and datapath. The chip combines two methods: CORDIC, a 1956 shift-and-add algorithm (invented by Jack Volder for B-58 bomber navigation) that uses precomputed angles arctan(2^-n) and needs no multiply or divide, and a Pade rational approximation 3x/(3-x^2) for the small residual angle. Sixteen CORDIC steps give about 16 bits of accuracy; the rational approximation, with error proportional to x^4 on an input under 2^-16, covers the rest to meet the 64-bit requirement. FPTAN returns numerator and denominator separately so the expensive division is avoided. The implementation runs in three microcode phases, pseudo-division (recording decision bits in a 16-bit shift register), the rational approximation (whose costliest operation is a 64-bit square via radix-4 Booth multiplication), and pseudo-multiplication applying rotations in reverse order. The article reports FPTAN taking roughly 90 microseconds against about 13,000 on the 8086, and notes the microcode ROM holds 1648 micro-instructions and that nonzero inputs always raise a precision exception.
novelty: die analysis shows 8087 hybrid CORDIC+polynomial tangent algorithm
audience: hardware archaeology/retrocomputing enthusiasts, chip reverse engineers

title: How To Write With An LLM
why: If you draft with an LLM, the piece gives you a usable discipline, never ship a phrase the model wrote, that keeps its tells out of your prose while still using it for grammar, fact-checking, and thesaurus work.
notes: Thomas Ptacek's 'Rule Number One': 'You may not use a single word an LLM suggests to you' — treat any specific turn of phrase the model offers as off limits, and be strict about it.
He frames the rule as 'intellectual personal protective equipment' against LLM-flavored prose; the idea is to accept the model's edits and critiques but write every actual word yourself.

Simon Willison endorses the approach and describes his own usage: fact-checking, spelling and grammar, and occasional thesaurus, with a dedicated proofreading prompt; he does not let LLMs write blog content.
Ptacek shows a screenshot of a personal LLM copyediting tool and provides a starter prompt for building your own; he later posted his full system prompt in a Hacker News comment.
This is an opinion/workflow post, not a study — no measurement of whether the rule actually removes detectable LLM style; it rests on Willison's subjective sense that LLM text 'has that weird smell.'
summary: Simon Willison's link-blog post highlights Thomas Ptacek's essay on using LLMs as copyeditors rather than writing assistants. Ptacek's central rule is that you may not use any specific word or turn of phrase an LLM suggests; he calls this 'intellectual personal protective equipment' against LLM-flavored prose, accepting the model's edits and feedback but writing all the words himself. Ptacek also demonstrates a personal LLM copyediting tool, offers a prompt for building one, and shared his system prompt in a Hacker News comment. Willison agrees with the rule and outlines his own practice: LLMs for fact-checking, spelling and grammar, and as an occasional thesaurus, but never to draft blog content, backed by a proofreading prompt. The piece is a workflow opinion rather than an empirical argument, resting on the subjective claim that LLM text has a recognizable 'smell.'
novelty: rule: never use an LLM's exact phrasing, only its edits
audience: writers and engineers using LLMs for editing/writing assistance

title: How to keep enjoying programming in a world of LLMs
why: If you delegate coding to agents, the author's warning is concrete: after a few weeks of handing everything off, you return to find your own coding ability and confidence degraded, so this is a worked alternative that keeps you writing the code while still spending tokens.
notes: Core inversion: refuse the standard harness pattern of plan-first-then-agent-codes; instead plan together but you write the code, and point the agent at everything else, especially boring, easy-to-check work (cleanup, low-risk refactors, swapping an unmaintained library, finishing the repetitive cases after you write the interesting ones).

On research, the agent is not there to decide for you: research in parallel with a plain search engine, make the agent write findings to disk with links to sources, and when it later proposes something odd ask which source backs it; the author estimates a 50% chance it catches its own mistake.

Borrows the GAN generator/discriminator framing for an automated review cycle: never read or accept any LLM artifact, code or plan, before a reviewer agent has no more findings; review catches cross-step plan holes (a function refactored in todo 2 but not written until todo 7).

Argues against relying on frontier-model features for four stated reasons: energy cost, accountability (you own the code, not the machine), token budgets that make big models an unreliable bet mid-session, and keeping the door open to open-weight/open-source replacements.

Reframes running out of tokens as a service outage at the whim of the vendor, not your overprovisioning; defense is caching tangible artifacts offline and always keeping a planned todo list you can work through without the agent.

Self-reported productivity gain is roughly 2x, offered as a loose estimate, lower than vibe-coder claims; all performance assertions (LLMs worse than advertised at readable code, skill loss within weeks) are the author's personal experience, not measured.
summary: A Haskell programmer's personal essay, stated to be fully human-written, arguing for a workflow that keeps the human writing the code while offloading everything around it to LLMs. The proposed split: use agents for bookkeeping, research organization, and todo/plan tracking (preferring markdown files with frontmatter over large context, which can silently drop information), but never let them author core code or make important decisions. The author inverts the usual plan-then-agent-codes harness: plan jointly, then write the code yourself, and run every LLM artifact, including plans, through an automated reviewer agent before reading it. He argues against depending on frontier models on grounds of energy cost, accountability, unpredictable token budgets, and future substitutability by open-weight models, and reframes token exhaustion as a vendor service outage to prepare for by caching work offline. Claims (LLMs worse than advertised at human-readable code, skill atrophy after a few weeks of full delegation, about 2x productivity) are self-reported rather than measured. He also urges meeting collaborators human-first, never sending fully generated PRs, and treating LLM output as tool output appended in a details block rather than communication.
novelty: personal workflow framework: LLMs for bookkeeping/research, not authored code
audience: working programmers worried about skill erosion and burnout from LLM coding agents

title: Anthropic's Scion is heavily inspired by Mononoke
why: When an LLM designs your next system, it will quietly reproduce the best open-source prior art without naming it, and here the author shows Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra themselves name the source Anthropic's post omitted.
notes: Anthropic's new VCS, Scion, uses a 'derived data' concept to speed operations like blame; the author shows this closely matches Meta's Mononoke source control server, which he helped build in 2017-18 and described using the same 'derived data' framing in 2022 Oxide candidate materials.

Anthropic's post credited Sapling only for 'hard-won lessons' and did not mention Mononoke at all; the author calls the omission bordering on plagiarism and reads the post as implying Claude originated the design.
Claim (self-reported, author): Mononoke is open source and in every LLM's training set, and asking Opus 5.5 or GPT-6 Astra about prior art yields an immediate pointer to Mononoke's similarities.
The author explicitly does not object to copying the design, which is why it was open-sourced, only to the missing attribution.
Mononoke itself borrowed from prior art, including Google's SrcFS and database write-ahead logs, which the author says his team credited.
No side-by-side code or spec diff is given beyond the shared 'derived data' concept and blame-efficiency goal; the plagiarism judgment rests on that overlap plus the LLMs' own attributions.
summary: The author, a former Meta engineer who helped build the Mononoke source control server (2017-18), argues that Anthropic's newly announced version control system, Scion, is heavily derived from Mononoke. He points to Scion's use of a 'derived data' concept to make operations like blame more efficient, matching how he described Mononoke's design in 2022, and notes Anthropic credited only Sapling for 'hard-won lessons' while omitting Mononoke entirely. He suggests Claude, trained on open-source Mononoke code, reproduced the design, and that the post reads as crediting Claude for the insights. He states he does not object to the copying, only to the lack of attribution, and claims that Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra both immediately identify Mononoke as prior art when asked. His broader point: as LLMs increasingly design systems by indexing on existing work, and because those same models make tracing prior art trivial, giving credit is now both easier and more necessary.
novelty: attribution dispute over Anthropic's Scion VCS design origins
audience: engineers interested in VCS internals, AI attribution ethics, and devtools history

title: Interactive refactoring in gopls
why: If you use gopls, struct-tag, interface-stub, and move-declaration refactorings now prompt for input instead of guessing, and the mechanism is a proposed LSP standard that could bring the same to every language server.
notes: Shipping now: gopls v0.24.0 and the VS Code Go extension v0.56.0; proof-of-concept client integrations explored for Neovim and Emacs.

The capability is proposed to the Language Server Protocol itself (microsoft/language-server-protocol#1164), co-designed with the Dart team as a cross-language standard, not a Go-only feature. Before this, the only LSP operation taking a parameter was rename, via a dedicated PrepareRename RPC.

Diagnosis: gopls could already compute the edits; the gap was LSP having no way for a server to ask the user for input, so 'Add struct tags' always emitted json tags in camelCase or the refactoring was not offered at all.

New/enabled refactorings: Add/Remove struct tags (choose tag keys like json,yaml,db and casing camelCase/snake_case/PascalCase), Implement Interface (golang/vscode-go#1547) with dynamic workspace+stdlib symbol autocomplete and prompts for type-parameter arguments, plus Change Signature (golang/go#38028) and Move Declaration (golang/go#70583).

Move Declaration is a preview (not yet in a release): it moves a top-level declaration plus only its dependent unexported helpers/methods, leaves unrelated symbols, updates references workspace-wide, and fixes imports in both files.

Roadmap items cited: change-signature across call sites, interactive conflict/shadowing resolution, and non-edit interactive commands such as configuring test/benchmark runs with CPU/memory/trace profiling flags. A 'Slay the dragon' action on a var named dragonSlayer ships as a client test case.
summary: The Go team introduced interactive refactoring in gopls, letting language servers collect multi-step user input before computing code edits. The underlying mechanism is a proposed Language Server Protocol capability (microsoft/language-server-protocol#1164), developed with the Dart team and pitched as an open, cross-language standard rather than a Go-specific extension; previously the only parameterized LSP operation was rename via PrepareRename. The post frames the prior limitation as protocol-level: gopls could compute edits but had no way to ask the user for input, so operations like 'Add struct tags' always produced json/camelCase tags or were omitted. Interactive versions now prompt for tag keys and naming conventions, let users remove specific tags, implement interfaces via dynamic workspace and standard-library symbol search with type-parameter argument prompts, and (in preview) move declarations across files and packages while carrying dependent symbols and fixing imports. Working support ships in gopls v0.24.0 and VS Code Go v0.56.0, with Neovim and Emacs proof-of-concept clients. The team lists change-signature refactoring, interactive conflict resolution, and interactive non-edit commands (such as profiling-flag configuration) on its roadmap.
novelty: LSP gains proposed multi-step dialog/parameter protocol, not just Go-specific
audience: Go developers and language server/editor tooling implementers

title: Banks are now trying to offload the AI data center debt they just underwrote
why: If the thread's claims hold, the banks that underwrote AI datacenter loans are now repricing that risk onto insurers at a discount, and a single hyperscaler's near-junk credit rating is already stalling billions in buildout.
notes: Bond yields cited in the thread: CoreWeave debt pushed toward 16%, Oracle toward 8% (reportedly 6% a week earlier). These are forum-stated figures, not sourced to filings.

The underwriting banks are said to be securitizing datacenter loans and selling the slices at a discount, with insurance companies named as the buyers chasing yield; a commenter frames this as routine commercial-real-estate practice (getting loans off balance sheets to avoid holding capital while keeping management fees), not necessarily a distress signal.

Specific stall claims, all unverified: Wisconsin's law requiring high credit rating or collateral for fast-tracked power projects allegedly blocks an Oracle datacenter's electricity; a New Mexico site stuck on water and gas-turbine contracts with Oracle invoking force majeure; Texas blocking new grid hookups over electricity-price backlash, killing an Oracle expansion. Oracle's July downgrade to near-junk is cited as the trigger.

A thread technical point worth keeping: unlike residential MBS bundling hundreds of small loans into risk tranches, datacenter loans are so large that a bond may hold only one or two, so tranching and diversification barely apply, and default events are correlated rather than independent when projects compete for the same power.

The core speculative theory, explicitly labeled personal opinion: Oracle taken private after a stock collapse, then acquired by OpenAI to wipe ~$500B in obligations and buy next-gen hardware cheaply, with creditors offered equity instead of cash. No evidence supports this.

Source is a Lemmy/HN comment thread (327 HN points), mixing a self-identified commercial-real-estate worker's explanation with heavy editorializing; treat all numbers and narratives as claims, not reporting.
summary: A Lemmy/Hacker News thread argues that the banks that underwrote AI datacenter construction loans are now securitizing and selling that debt, reportedly at a discount, with insurance companies as the main buyers. Commenters cite bond yields moving against borrowers (CoreWeave toward 16%, Oracle toward 8%) and tie the risk to Oracle's July downgrade to near-junk, which they say is stalling datacenter projects in Wisconsin, New Mexico, and Texas over power, water, and grid-hookup constraints. One contributor who works in commercial real estate frames loan securitization as standard bank practice for shedding capital requirements while keeping fees, and notes that datacenter loans are too large and too few per bond to tranche or diversify like residential MBS, making correlated default a real concern. Much of the thread is explicit speculation, including a theory that Oracle is a 'sacrificial lamb' to be taken private and absorbed by OpenAI to erase debt and acquire cheap hardware. None of the figures or project claims are sourced to filings or primary reporting, so they should be read as forum assertions rather than verified facts.
novelty: banks offloading AI datacenter debt to insurers amid credit downgrades
audience: investors and engineers tracking AI infrastructure financing risk
